summary: OrbitSight is a browser-based offline research prototype that helps astronauts turn a vision concern into a clear next step. Inspired by Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome, it combines guided vision observations with a medical review workflow and an experiment in mission readability tasks and does not depend on assumed AI prescriptions. The interface provides adjustable screen calibration, a handover preview and a simulated non drug care plan for crew members who may not be doctors. Its distinctive idea is to compare standard and more readable task presentations, examining whether display changes could support task performance. NASA resources inform the health focus and intended care pathway. The Evidence Explorer identifies OSD-817 as laboratory research context, with source file analysis still pending. Crew records are synthetic, and the prototype does not diagnose disease or issue prescriptions. Our next step is to verify persistent case management and measurement quality before usability and clinical evaluation.
details:
Problem and purpose

OrbitSight addresses the challenge of helping astronauts gather health indicators, understand their significance and take an appropriate next step. We focus on vision because NASA identifies Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome as a concern for long duration missions. Vision changes can affect the ability to read instructions and displays. Our question is practical: how can a crew member who is not a doctor record a concern and communicate it clearly for medical review?

How the prototype works

The browser interface offers a guided observation sequence with an adjustable screen-calibration line, viewing-distance input and explicit setup confirmations. A dashboard presents synthetic observations and an open review case. It directs the crew member to contact the Crew Medical Officer without waiting for another test. Help Now opens a handover preview that distinguishes available information from missing information. The Care Plan page illustrates a non drug follow-up plan with plain-language instructions and a named responder.

The Crew Member, Crew Medical Officer and Flight Surgeon selections demonstrate different participants in the intended pathway. They are simulation controls, not verified clinical identities. In an operational system, clinical personnel or a valid mission protocol would authorize care. OrbitSight would present those instructions and support follow-up. The current prototype does not generate diagnoses, medicines, doses or prescriptions.

Creative contribution

Task readability connects health observations with an activity the crew must perform: reading a mission style checklist. It provides standard and more readable task presentations, starts new attempts with blank responses and avoids declaring an improvement before both attempts exist. The proposed evaluation compares completion time, errors and omissions using equivalent tasks and counterbalanced order. This could help identify useful display adjustments while keeping medical decisions separate.
Disclaimer: No performance improvement has yet been measured or established.

NASA resources and design choices

NASA SANS resources guide our health focus. NASA medical training and medical operations guidance inform the human review pathway. We select OSD-817, Optic Nerve Tilt, for a narrowly scoped Evidence Explorer. The current implementation identifies the study and its provenance. Workbook verification and quantitative analysis remain pending. Laboratory tissue data do not serve as astronaut telemetry or as a basis for clinical thresholds.

Impact and current limits

The intended benefits are clearer symptom reporting, more complete handovers and instructions that non-clinical crew members can follow. A browser based approach could reuse available displays and reduce extra hardware needs, although cost, energy use and accessibility have not been formally measured. The deployed prototype uses synthetic crew records. Persistent case management, communication-state retention, reviewer authorization, exports and offline reliability require further work. We will verify these functions and test usability with appropriate medical input before considering clinical evaluation. The project makes no claim of diagnostic accuracy, treatment effectiveness or operational readiness.

Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions. Our response concentrates on guided vision observations, medical review and task readability rather than attempting to cover every astronaut health condition.
